Stablecoins: what keeps them stable, and what happens when they are not

A stablecoin tries to stay worth one unit of a currency, usually one US dollar. Many people use them to avoid price swings, but stable does not mean risk free.

Three common types

  • Backed by reserves. The issuer says it holds cash or similar assets for each coin. You trust the issuer and its reports.
  • Backed by crypto. Other crypto is locked as collateral, usually more than the coins issued. It depends on the code and on prices.
  • Algorithmic. The price is held by code and market confidence, with little or no real backing. This is the riskiest type, and several have collapsed.

What can go wrong

  • Depeg. The price falls below the target, for example to 0.90 dollars, and may not come back.
  • Issuer problems. The issuer may not have the reserves it claims, or may freeze certain addresses.
  • Platform or bridge failure. The place that holds your coins can fail even if the coin itself is fine.
  • Fake coins. A token can copy the name and logo of a real stablecoin.
  • Wrong network. Sending to a network the receiver does not support can lose the funds.

A short checklist

  1. Find the coin on CoinGecko and compare its contract address with the one on the issuer's official website.
  2. Look at the price history over the past year. Repeated dips below the target are a warning.
  3. Read how the backing is described. Is there a clear explanation and are there regular reports by outside parties?
  4. Do not keep all your savings in one coin or one place. Spread the risk.
  5. Check that you can actually sell it for local money in your country, and what that costs.

A stablecoin is not a bank account

Bank deposits often have insurance and clear rules. Most stablecoins do not. Treat a stablecoin as a tool for moving and holding value for a short time, and do not assume someone will cover your loss if it fails. Nothing here is financial advice.

Tools mentioned in this guide

  • CoinGecko

    Prices, market caps and basic data for thousands of coins.

    How to start (5 steps)
    1. Open the CoinGecko website and type the token's name or ticker in the search box.
    2. Pick the result with the right name and symbol. Fake tokens copy names, so compare the contract address on the page with the one the project publishes on its own website.
    3. Look at market cap, 24-hour trading volume and the number of markets. Very low volume, or one tiny market, means a single trade can move the price.
    4. Use the official website and social links listed on the token page, not links sent to you in a chat.
    5. Open the price chart with the longest range to see the whole history, and check which exchanges list the token.

    CoinGecko shows data. It does not tell you whether a token is safe or will rise.

    Level: Beginner
    Open CoinGecko (opens in a new tab)

  • DefiLlama

    DeFi protocol rankings, TVL and chain data in one place.

    How to start (5 steps)
    1. Open DefiLlama and look at the DeFi rankings by TVL (total value locked).
    2. Click a project and check how its TVL changed over time and on which blockchains it runs.
    3. Watch for sudden drops, or TVL that is mostly the project's own token. That can look bigger than it is.
    4. Look for audit and past hack information on the page, and check the stablecoin and chain pages for context.
    5. Treat very high yields with suspicion. High yield usually means high risk.

    TVL measures how much is deposited. It does not measure how safe a project is.

    Level: Beginner
    Open DefiLlama (opens in a new tab)
